International Policy Conference

2027 Finals in Boston, Massachusetts, USA

About the International Policy Confernece

The International Policy Conference, or IPC, was established in 2026 by a group of Harvard students and graduates in hopes of providing exposure to global perspectives to future leaders early in their education. We strive to encourage students to take some of the problems they might have seen in their communities and ask not just “what is the problem” but “why does it persist, how can we solve it, and who can we work with to change it.” IPC challenges students by delving deep into fields they might never have encountered in school, such as economics, international law, public health, environmental science, and more. In the process of developing research, synthesis, public speaking, negotiation, and persuasive communication skills, students will be given the unique opportunity to get their policy recommendations to the legislators whose vote influences real-world outcomes in their communities.

Eight Policy Categories

Health

Healthcare financing, pharmaceutical regulation, mental health infrastructure, public health preparedness, and insurance market design

Education

School funding equity, higher education access, early childhood development, curriculum policy, and teacher workforce.

Environmental

Climate mitigation, carbon pricing, biodiversity regulation, environmental justice, and international climate governance

International Relations

Foreign policy, arms control, multilateral institutions, humanitarian law, refugee policy, and non-proliferation.

Economic & Fiscal

Tax policy, public expenditure, labor markets, trade policy, income inequality, and macroeconomic stabilization.

Housing & Urban

Affordable housing production, zoning and land use, homelessness, urban infrastructure, and community development.

AI & Technology

AI regulation, data privacy, algorithmic accountability, platform governance, cybersecurity, and digital infrastructure.

Civil Rights

Policing policy, sentencing reform, juvenile justice, voting rights, civil liberties, and anti-discrimination law.

Overview of International Policy Conference Stages

Stage I: Topic Foundation
Submit a polished 500‑word Topic Statement outlining your policy challenge, its global relevance, and your intended analytical approach. Must be enrolled at an IPO‑registered affiliate school and complete registration or waiver approval.
Stage II: Policy Brief
Submit a full policy brief by December 15, 2026. Regional evaluation identifies the top 20% of briefs demonstrating exceptional empirical reasoning, clarity, and feasibility.
Stage III: National Pitch
Produce a concise, high‑impact video pitch by April 30, 2027. National panels evaluate communication strength, analytical depth, and policy innovation. Up to five finalists per country advance.
Stage IV: International Finals
Finalists complete verification and receive national selection confirmation. Attendance at the Cambridge program is required, where students present to global policy experts, participate in workshops, and compete for international distinction.

Requirements by Stage

Formatting Specifications

  • Word count: 1,500–2,500 words, body text only. Title, headings, executive summary, appendices, tables, figures, and citations are excluded.
  • File format: PDF only. Filename: LastName_Country_Category_IPO2027.pdf
  • Font: 11–12pt. Minimum 1-inch margins. Single or 1.15 line spacing.
  • Tables and figures must be numbered and captioned, with data sources cited in the caption.
  • All statistical claims must cite a primary source: government data, peer-reviewed study, or a recognized international body (WHO, World Bank, OECD, or equivalent).
  • Citations: APA 7th or Chicago 17th edition. Minimum 8 sources; at least 4 must be primary or peer-reviewed.
  • Appendices are permitted and excluded from the word count, but should not contain material integral to the core argument.

Mandatory Brief Structure

  • Executive Summary (150 words max): State the problem, proposed intervention, and expected primary outcome in jargon-free prose.
  • Problem Definition and Scope: Define the problem with at least one quantitative indicator of its magnitude. Specify jurisdiction and time horizon.
  • Background and Context: Summarize the relevant policy history and prior interventions. Cite at least three independent sources.
  • Stakeholder Analysis: Identify at least three distinct stakeholder groups; describe each group's interest, influence, and how the proposed policy affects them.
  • Policy Options: Present at minimum two distinct approaches evaluated against the same criteria: cost, feasibility, equity, and evidence base.
  • Recommended Policy: State the preferred approach, implementing authority, and a realistic implementation timeline.
  • Anticipated Objections: Address at least two significant objections with substantive responses.
  • References: Full bibliography. Minimum 8 sources; at least 4 primary or peer-reviewed.

Academic Integrity Requirements

  • All submissions are screened for plagiarism. A match rate above 15 percent (excluding the reference list) will trigger manual review and may result in disqualification.
  • Use of AI language model tools to draft or substantively write any portion of a policy brief is not permitted. Students certify at submission that all written work is entirely their own. Submissions are subject to AI detection screening.
  • Faculty advisors may assist students in identifying sources and reviewing argument structure, but may not draft, substantially edit, or revise student text. The advisor role is analogous to a research supervisor, not a co-author.
  • Students must disclose any familial, professional, or personal connection to organizations cited or analyzed in their brief. Failure to disclose constitutes a conflict of interest violation.

Technical Specifications

  • Duration: 8 minutes minimum, 12 minutes maximum. Videos outside this range are disqualified without review.
  • Format: MP4 or MOV, minimum 720p (1280×720). Audio must be clear and free of significant background noise.
  • File size: Maximum 2GB. Submit via IPO upload portal only; external platform links are not accepted.
  • Students may appear on camera, narrate over slides, or combine both; no requirement for on-camera presentation.
  • Submissions must be in English. Students may include subtitles but must present in English.
  • No background music, dramatic effects, or theatrical elements.

Required Content Elements

  • Opening statement (approx. 90 sec): Identify the policy problem and state at least one quantitative measure of its scale or severity. Lead with evidence.
  • Policy proposal (approx. 2–3 min): Identify the implementing authority, target population, and primary mechanism of effect.
  • Evidence base (approx. 2 min): Cite at least two independent studies or data sources. Distinguish correlational from causal evidence where relevant.
  • Objections and trade-offs (approx. 2 min): Address at least one significant objection and describe the primary limitation or equity concern.
  • Conclusion (approx. 60 sec): State the primary expected outcome and the condition under which it is most likely to be achieved.

Live Pitch Requirements

  • Duration: 12 minutes. Timing is enforced; finalists will be signaled at 10 minutes and stopped at 12.
  • Slides or visual materials must be submitted to the organizing committee by 9:00 PM the evening before the presentation slot.
  • All team members must be present at the podium. Speaking responsibilities may be divided at the team's discretion.
  • Finalists must present from memory or notes; reading verbatim from a prepared text is not permitted.
  • Presentations will be recorded for the competition archive. Recording constitutes consent for non-commercial use by IPO.

Executive Q&A Format

  • Duration: 15 minutes, moderated by the IPO Chair of Proceedings.
  • The executive panel may ask any question related to the proposal, evidence cited, analytical methodology, or implementation.
  • Questions may be adversarial; panel members may adopt a skeptical position regardless of their personal views.
  • Students may consult their notes and submitted brief during Q&A. No external materials or devices are permitted.
  • Team members may confer briefly (under 30 seconds) before responding.
  • Responses should be direct and concise. Non-responsive answers are evaluated negatively regardless of length.

Updated Policy Summary (Stage IV Requirement)

All finalists must submit a 500-word updated policy summary on Day 2, due by 11:59 PM local time. Required elements: the policy recommendation in one sentence; the three strongest pieces of supporting evidence; the primary implementation challenge; and the proposed metric by which the policy's effectiveness should be evaluated within five years. This document is provided to the executive judges prior to the Day 3 Q&A session.

International Finals
The International Conference
The international finals take place over three days in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Finalists present their proposals before an executive panel composed of sitting legislators and senior government officials.
Executive Judge Panel
Harvard professors and faculty, U.S. senators, members of Congress, state legislators, and senior federal officials evaluate and cross‑examine finalists on the empirical rigor and feasibility of their proposals.
Legislative Committee Format
The 15‑minute Q&A replicates a congressional committee hearing. Panelists may interrupt, challenge assumptions, and request clarification on specific empirical claims.
Policy Symposium
A two‑day symposium runs alongside the competition, featuring sessions led by policy researchers, faculty, and practitioners across multiple disciplines.
Awards & Policy Transmission
Category awards and the Grand Award are presented on June 15. Select proposals may be formally transmitted to legislative committees for further consideration.

FAQ Section
Frequently Asked Questions
Does the policy proposal have to concern U.S. policy?
No. Students may analyze policy questions at any jurisdictional level. Proposals addressing policies in their home country, a foreign jurisdiction, or a multilateral body are all acceptable.
Is AI writing assistance permitted?
AI tools may not be used to draft or substantively write any submitted text. Formatting, citation checking, and data retrieval uses are allowed.
Can students from countries without an IPO affiliate participate?
Yes. Students may register through the international enrollment process, which assigns them to the appropriate regional pool.
Are travel costs covered for international finalists?
Accommodation is provided for all finalists. A travel grant program is available for students with financial need.
What distinguishes IPO from a policy debate competition?
IPO emphasizes original research and analysis rather than rhetorical advocacy. Students defend their own policy recommendations.
How are categories assigned for interdisciplinary proposals?
Students are placed in the category that best matches the primary policy domain of their proposal.
How does blind review work at Stage II?
All briefs are anonymized before judging. Each is reviewed by at least three independent experts.
Can a school enter students in multiple categories?
Yes. Schools may enter any number of students across categories. Each student may compete in only one category per year.
